clue.text: They steal before they rob, it seems

definitions.text: They steal before they rob, it seems

parts.words: They steal before they rob, it seems
parts.note: read 'steal' as creeping softly along on foot: old highway robbers who went on foot, not horseback, padded up to their victims before robbing them

explanation.surface: A remark that thieves must first steal in order to rob.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Steal' looks like theft, but here it means move stealthily, as the old foot-going robbers did before holding someone up.
explanation.definitionFit: These were highway robbers who worked on foot rather than mounted, a historical term for street thieves.

clue.text: One's seen in crossings, but they're too deep to wade

indicators.note: seen in means the numeral is placed within the word for crossings

parts.note: fords are shallow river crossings
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: Fords are crossings, but these waters are too deep to wade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'seen in' puts I (one) inside FORDS; 'but' links to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: These are deep, narrow sea inlets between cliffs, far too deep for wading, unlike a ford.

clue.text: Revels that put some service man in sore distress

indicators.note: in places the serviceman inside the rearranged word
to distress something is to damage or roughen it, so the word sore is knocked about

parts.note: taken as written
a GI is an American soldier

explanation.surface: Wild parties that leave a serviceman in painful trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'distress' makes ORES, and 'in' is the container signal; a GI is a US serviceman, and 'some' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: Orgies are wild drunken celebrations, a stronger word for revelries.

clue.text: Wordy wisecrack and a sharp blow I get from an Oriental

parts.note: a pun is a joke playing on words
a jab is a short sharp punch

explanation.surface: Someone receives a verbal quip and a punch from a man from the East.
explanation.definitionFit: A Punjabi is a native of the Punjab in South Asia, someone from the East in this old usage.

clue.text: The tiny coin belongs to you, tiny man-so take a tip from Smiles

parts.note: a doit was a small old Dutch coin of very low value
what belongs to you is yours
an elf is a tiny sprite

explanation.surface: A small coin is yours, little fellow, so follow Smiles's advice.
explanation.walkthrough: Samuel Smiles wrote the Victorian bestseller 'Self-Help', so his tip is to manage on your own.
explanation.definitionFit: Smiles preached self-reliance, which is the advice to handle tasks personally without hiring help.

clue.text: Biblical rider comes to Welsh lake before noon

parts.note: Bala is the largest natural lake in Wales
a.m. stands for ante meridiem, before midday

explanation.surface: A rider from the Bible arrives at a lake in Wales one morning.
explanation.walkthrough: BALA is Llyn Tegid, the largest natural lake in Wales; 'comes to' only links the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Book of Numbers the prophet rode an ass that spoke to him, making him the Bible's best-known rider.

clue.text: Pays out on account of churchman in a long time

indicators.note: in puts the churchman's title inside the long time

parts.note: ages is a long time
Ven. abbreviates Venerable, an archdeacon's title

explanation.surface: A clergyman takes ages over handing out money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pays out' means takes revenge, not disburses money; VEN is the abbreviation for Venerable, an archdeacon's title.
explanation.definitionFit: To pay someone out is to get even with them, which is taking revenge.

clue.text: Curvaceous bee-skeps, say the records

indicators.note: say signals that the phrase is spoken, giving a sound like the answer

parts.note: arched beehives: a skep is a domed straw hive, and arch means curved

explanation.surface: Curved straw beehives are said to be the records.
explanation.walkthrough: Spoken, 'arch hives' runs together into the answer; skeps are old domed straw beehives.
explanation.definitionFit: Archives are collections of historical records and documents.

clue.text: Who welcomes us to the pit for a pint ?

definitions.text: Who welcomes us to the pit for a pint ?

parts.words: Who welcomes us to the pit for a pint ?
parts.note: a pit is a mine, and the one who welcomes us is a host; together they make the jovial old name for a pub landlord serving pints

explanation.surface: Someone welcoming visitors to a colliery for a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the pit' gives MINE and 'who welcomes us' gives HOST, but the whole is the jocular term for an innkeeper.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a jocular old way of addressing a pub landlord or innkeeper.

clue.text: Die after many pipes of this stuff ?

indicators.note: after places the word die behind the instrument of many pipes

parts.note: a church organ is an instrument of many pipes

explanation.surface: Someone asks what material would perish after many pipes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Die' looks like a verb of perishing but is just the word itself, placed last by 'after'; 'this stuff' points to a material.
explanation.definitionFit: Organdie is a fine stiff muslin, a fabric, so it is a kind of material or cloth.

clue.text: High hill on a pavement

definitions.meaning: a hill on which signal fires were lit
a Belisha ... is the flashing orange globe on a post at the pavement's edge by a zebra crossing

explanation.surface: A tall hill standing on a pavement, a deliberately odd picture.
explanation.walkthrough: A Belisha beacon is the British flashing amber globe that marks a zebra (pedestrian) crossing, set on the pavement.
explanation.definitionFit: Signal-fire hills bear this name, as does the flashing globe on a pole at British pedestrian crossings.

clue.text: The country's top people emerging from Heathrow?

definitions.meaning: the gentry who own rural estates
people who have come in on a plane at the airport, having touched down

explanation.surface: Upper-class people coming out of London's main airport.
explanation.walkthrough: Heathrow is London's main airport, so its arrivals have just landed.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names estate-owning country families, and literally describes nobility just off a plane.

clue.text: Food to cause-to expire thankfully on the railway

parts.note: to expire is to die
ta is British slang for thank you
RY is the abbreviation for railway

explanation.surface: A garbled-sounding note about food and dying gratefully on a train.
explanation.walkthrough: TA is informal British for 'thanks'; 'to cause' and 'on' only join the pieces in this old clue.
explanation.definitionFit: As a noun this means a regulated course of meals or allowance of provisions.

clue.text: His gun a possible cause of suffering

indicators.note: a possible arrangement of the words his gun a is one of the ways their letters could be reordered

explanation.surface: A man's gun might cause someone pain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possible' signals that HIS GUN A is rearranged; 'cause of' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: Anguish is severe mental or physical pain, a synonym for suffering.

clue.text: Money to be spent like Water?

definitions.meaning: cash and holdings readily available for spending
read literally, things that are fluid like water

explanation.surface: Money that gets spent like water, as the saying goes.
explanation.definitionFit: Accountants call cash and readily convertible holdings by this name; taken literally it means fluid possessions.

clue.text: General Jumbo user

definitions.meaning: Jumbo was a famous elephant, standing for elephants generally; this commander took them over the Alps

explanation.definitionFit: The Carthaginian commander famously crossed the Alps with war elephants against Rome.

clue.text: Kind of dance for which the sergeant wears a blazer?

parts.note: a flame is something that blazes
a sergeant is an NCO, a non-commissioned officer

explanation.surface: A dance in which the sergeant puts on a sports jacket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'blazer' looks like a jacket but means a thing that blazes; 'wears' only links the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Flamenco is a passionate Spanish Andalusian style of dancing.

clue.text: Dan loads fuel abruptly

annotationWithheld.why: Dan loads fuel abruptly (3,2,1,6): DAN LOADS FUEL is rearranged with no word signalling the anagram, so the wordplay has no indicator the check can accept

clue.text: Fireplace with ash container in front

indicators.note: in sets the ash container within the word for front

parts.note: the face is the front
an urn holds cremation ashes

explanation.surface: A hearth with an ash urn standing before it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in front' looks like position, but 'in' is the container signal and 'front' is FACE.
explanation.definitionFit: A furnace is an enclosed chamber where fire is kept burning to give heat.

clue.text: Take a dekko northwards from King's Lynn: it's deceptive

parts.note: dekko is British slang for a look, so to eye
the Wash is the bay lying just north of King's Lynn in Norfolk

explanation.surface: Look north from King's Lynn and the view is misleading.
explanation.walkthrough: King's Lynn is a Norfolk town at the head of the Wash, a broad North Sea bay; 'dekko' is British slang for a look.
explanation.definitionFit: Eyewash is talk meant to mislead, humbug or nonsense.

clue.text: A lad and Una cuddle in the carriage

indicators.note: to cuddle is to squeeze up together, so the two names are mixed into one huddle

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A boy and a girl named Una snuggle in a horse-drawn carriage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cuddle' mixes LAD and UNA together; 'A', 'and' and 'in' only link.
explanation.definitionFit: A landau is a four-wheeled horse-drawn carriage with a folding hood.

clue.text: Darwin's " Rover "

parts.note: the ship that carried Darwin on his roving voyage round the world, named after a breed of hound, and Rover is a stock dog's name

explanation.surface: Charles Darwin's pet dog.
explanation.walkthrough: Rover looks like a dog, which the answer also is, but it also means the vessel on which Darwin roved the world.
explanation.definitionFit: HMS Beagle carried Darwin on his voyage of 1831-36, and the name is also a breed of hunting hound.

clue.text: A number of Ural men

annotationWithheld.why: A number of Ural men (7): URAL MEN is rearranged with no word signalling the anagram, so the wordplay has no indicator the check can accept

clue.text: Raise cheer

definitions.meaning: to lift up to a higher position

explanation.definitionFit: Elevate means lift physically and also lift in spirits, as an elevating speech does.

clue.text: Box cock ?

definitions.meaning: to box at the weight class just above flyweight
a small breed of domestic fowl, the cock of which is noted for pugnacity

explanation.definitionFit: A boxing weight division and a small breed of fowl share this name.

clue.text: " Rover " indeed

parts.note: Rover is a stock name for a pet dog, and a dog that roves is one that has wandered from home

explanation.surface: Rover, a dog's name, is a fitting one.
explanation.walkthrough: Rover is a traditional name for a dog; 'indeed' asks for a dog that really roves.
explanation.definitionFit: A dog that wanders without a home is a true rover, so the stock pet name fits it literally.

clue.text: Lily is embracing one of this name

indicators.note: embracing means holding inside, so the pet name wraps around the word one

parts.note: Lil is a short pet form of the name Lily
taken as written

explanation.surface: Lily is hugging someone who bears a particular name.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is embracing' is the container signal; the definition is only 'this name', with 'of' a link, since the answer is a man's first name.
explanation.definitionFit: Lionel is a masculine given name, so it is the name the clue points to.

clue.text: Sussex building plot ? It's built up

parts.note: Rye is a town in East Sussex
a house is a building

explanation.surface: A Sussex building plot, which is then built up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'building plot' suggests land for development; the plot is the Rye House Plot of 1683 against Charles II. 'It's built up' points at a house being built.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1683 conspiracy to assassinate Charles II and his brother is named after this Hertfordshire residence.
